bib.title: ClashEval: Quantifying the tug-of-war between an LLM's internal prior and external evidence
bib.venue: NeurIPS 2024 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks (arXiv v3, 7 Feb 2025)

read.skipped: Figures 1-6 are images; only captions read, plotted values not read. References skimmed.

question: When retrieved context conflicts with an LLM's own prior answer, does the model keep the correct one, and how does this depend on the model's prior confidence and how far the context deviates from the truth?
hypothesis: Models are more likely to adopt context when they are less confident in their prior and when the context deviates less from the truth; token probabilities can therefore be used to arbitrate.
contributions: ClashEval, a QA benchmark of over 1200 questions across six domains with a relevant document each, the answer perturbed from subtle to extreme.
Benchmark of six LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, Llama-3-8b-instruct, Gemini 1.5, Claude Opus, Claude Sonnet) on three metrics.
Analysis of context preference rate against perturbation degree and against prior token probability (three models).
A simple token-probability correction that improves performance on ClashEval.

method.summary: GPT-4o generates question/answer/excerpt triples from web pages in six domains; the answer in the document is perturbed at 3 or 10 levels. Each model answers once without context (prior) and once with the (possibly wrong) context, and the response is scored against the right answer, the perturbed answer, or neither. Token log-probabilities of the response are used for a post-hoc correction.
method.task: short-answer QA with retrieved context that is correct or deliberately corrupted

datasets.name: Drug Dosage
datasets.source: 500 randomly sampled UpToDate.com drug pages; GPT-4o question generation then GPT-4o quality filter
datasets.preprocessing: answer constrained to a numeric value in mg

datasets.name: News
datasets.source: Associated Press RSS top headlines 03/15/24 to 03/25/24; 1486 articles, one question each
datasets.preprocessing: GPT-4o asked for a clear numerical answer; second GPT-4o quality-control step

datasets.name: Wikipedia Dates
datasets.preprocessing: answer must be a four-digit year; excerpt must appear exactly in the context

datasets.name: Sports Records
datasets.preprocessing: records taken from tables; one question per record entry

datasets.name: Names
datasets.preprocessing: answer must be first and last name

datasets.name: Locations
datasets.preprocessing: city names stripped of other identifiers (Seattle, not Seattle, WA)

other.use: generates questions, quality-control filter, and perturbed excerpts for drug dosages and news

inference.samples: one prior response and one contextual response per question and perturbation; no repeats or seeds stated
inference.prompting: standard RAG prompt template based on LangChain and LlamaIndex RAG prompts; also 'strict' and 'loose' variants (Fig 6); full prompts only in the GitHub repository
inference.retrieval: no retriever: one gold document per question with the answer replaced; multi-document variant adds four more documents chosen by embedding cosine similarity (k=5), embedding model not named

parameters.years_offsets: ten absolute modifications in increments of 20 years over [-100, 100] (Wikipedia Years)
parameters.token_prob_correction: if mean token probability of the no-context response exceeds that of the with-context response, return the no-context response, else the context response
parameters.calibrated_correction: same comparison but on percentiles of each probability distribution rather than raw probabilities

other.prior_probability: average log probability of the response tokens queried without context (Fig 4 caption)
other.answer_matching: how a response is judged right, wrong or neither is not described in the text

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.definition: Pr[r(q|c) right | c right or r(q) right]

metrics.name: Prior Bias
metrics.definition: Pr[r(q|c) wrong | c right and r(q) wrong]; model keeps its prior while context is correct

metrics.name: Context Bias
metrics.definition: Pr[r(q|c) wrong | c wrong and r(q) right]; model uses the context while the prior is correct

metrics.name: Context preference rate
metrics.definition: proportion of responses that align with the information in the prompt as context

baselines: random replacement of the final answer with the prior at the same 8.5% bias rate
eval.protocol: 95% confidence intervals reported in tables (method not named); linear fits for Fig 3 and 4; correction methods tested on the three models that expose token probabilities

availability.data: ClashEval dataset open-sourced at the same repository; document text may be under copyright so code to reproduce the data is supplied

evidence.where: Section 3.1; the contributions list says Llama-3-8b-instruct

evidence.quote: we compare the percentiles rather than raw probability scores

results.claim: GPT-4o adopts incorrect retrieved content over 60% of the time when its own prior was right (headline, as printed in abstract and Discussion).
results.setup: ClashEval, GPT-4o, subset where only the prior is correct, standard prompt, all perturbation levels pooled
results.quote: overriding their own correct prior knowledge over 60% of the time
results.table: Table 2, row GPT-4o, Context, column Prior Correct
results.note: The abstract does not name a model; the Discussion attributes it to GPT-4o. The 0.608 is the Table 2 'Context chosen' rate. The context-bias metric for the same model in Tables 3 and 4 is 0.304, exactly half; every model shows the same 2x ratio (Opus 0.313 vs 0.157, Sonnet 0.401 vs 0.201, Gemini 0.490 vs 0.245, GPT-3.5 0.626 vs 0.313, Llama-3 0.529 vs 0.264). Also, only GPT-3.5 (0.626) exceeds 60% in that Table 2 column besides GPT-4o, so 'over 60%' is not true of the six models in general. The paper does not explain the factor of two (derived by the reader).

results.claim: Claude Opus is best on all three metrics: accuracy 0.743, context bias 0.157, prior bias 0.021.
results.quote: with an accuracy of 74.3%, a context bias of 15.7%, and a prior bias of 2.1%

results.setup: ClashEval, standard prompt, one run per model
results.note: Table 3 baseline for GPT-4o accuracy 0.615 matches; its CI (0.595, 0.636) differs slightly from Table 4 CI (0.594, 0.633).

results.claim: Llama-3 and GPT-3.5 are near random at deciding between prior and context.
results.quote: models like Llama-3 and GPT-3.5 are at near random accuracy

results.claim: Calibrated token-probability correction raises GPT-4o accuracy from 0.615 to 0.754 and cuts context bias from 0.304 to 0.107, at the cost of prior bias rising 0.021 to 0.085.
results.setup: GPT-4o, percentile-compared token probabilities of no-context vs with-context response
results.table: Table 3, row GPT-4o, Calibrated Token Prob. Correction (0.754, 0.107, 0.085); baseline 0.615, 0.304, 0.021

results.claim: Uncalibrated token-probability correction for GPT-4o: accuracy 0.693, context bias 0.194, prior bias 0.043.
results.setup: GPT-4o, raw mean token probabilities compared
results.table: Table 3, row GPT-4o, Token Probability Correction (0.693, 0.194, 0.043)

results.claim: GPT-3.5: baseline 0.539/0.313/0.028; token prob correction 0.596/0.253/0.056; calibrated 0.701/0.110/0.147 (accuracy/context bias/prior bias).
Llama-3: baseline 0.500/0.264/0.021; token prob correction 0.556/0.235/0.046; calibrated 0.649/0.111/0.188 (accuracy/context bias/prior bias).
results.note: Text says calibrated correction raises accuracy 'by 14%' and prior bias goes 'from 2% to 8.5%'; 8.5% is GPT-4o only. Prior bias for GPT-3.5 (0.147) and Llama-3 (0.188) is much higher.

results.claim: At the same 8.5% prior-bias rate, a random replace-with-prior baseline reaches 57.5% accuracy against 75.4% for the calibrated method.
results.quote: the random baseline has an accuracy of 57.5%
results.note: Text does not name the model; 75.4% and 8.5% match GPT-4o in Table 3.

results.claim: Context preference falls as the prior token probability rises; per-dataset slopes range from -0.1 to -0.45.
results.metric: slope of context preference vs prior probability
results.setup: models exposing token probabilities, ten probability bins, linear fit per dataset; Dates most susceptible, News most robust
results.quote: a slope of -0.45, for instance, can be interpreted as expecting a 4.5% decrease in the likelihood of the LLM preferring the contextual information for every 10% increase in the probability of the model

results.claim: Context preference falls as the context deviates more from truth; Claude Opus adheres to incorrect context 30% less than GPT-4o at the same degree of modification.
results.setup: linear fit of context preference vs deviation (Fig 3), Opus vs GPT-4o
results.quote: Claude Opus adheres to incorrect contextual information 30% less than GPT-4o for the same degrees of modification
results.note: Fig 3 values not read; only the text claim.

results.claim: Prompt wording changes context preference: a 'strict' prompt enforcing literal adherence gives higher context preference than a 'loose' prompt that allows judgment; the loose prompt gives lower, steeper drops. Only shown as curves, no numbers.
results.metric: context preference rate vs prior probability
results.setup: Fig 6, model labelled 'GPT-4' in the caption (not GPT-4o), strict vs loose vs standard prompts; prompts are in the GitHub repo
results.quote: We observe lower and steeper drops in context preference with the loose vs strict prompts
results.note: Section 3.1 cites the result as 'results in 6'; the experiment is in Figure 6 in the appendix. Standard prompt is not described as plotted in the caption.

results.claim: Adding four more documents (k=5) lowers accuracy, raises neither-chosen, and lowers context bias: GPT-4o context chosen when prior correct 0.582 (k=1) to 0.383 (k=5); Claude Opus 0.287 to 0.237.
results.setup: GPT-4o and Claude Opus, four extra documents by embedding cosine similarity
results.quote: adding more contextual documents lowers overall model accuracy and increases the rate of responses that are neither the prior nor the context
results.table: Table 7, GPT-4o k=5 vs k=1, row Context Chosen, column Prior Correct
results.note: Table 7 k=1 values (0.582, 0.287) differ from Table 2 (0.608, 0.313) for the same models.

results.claim: With correct context, accuracy across all domains (k=1 vs k=5): GPT-4o 0.941 vs 0.922; Claude Opus 0.939 vs 0.843; without context 0.467 and 0.463.
results.setup: Claude Opus, All row, k=5 vs k=1

results.claim: Accuracy without context vs with correct context, all domains (Table 5): GPT-4o 0.467 vs 0.941; GPT-3.5 0.344 vs 0.879; Llama 3 0.228 vs 0.805. News is nearly unanswerable without context (GPT-4o 0.0882).
results.setup: GPT-4o, All row; mean prior prob 0.675

results.claim: Model size: the paper runs no scaling experiment and reports no effect of parameter count. It says GPT-4o has higher context bias than 'smaller models like Claude Sonnet', and Llama-3 (the only open, small model) has lower context bias than GPT-4o but lower accuracy because it more often picks neither.
results.setup: parameter counts of the commercial models are not given
results.note: Sonnet is only called smaller by the authors; no sizes are stated.

limits: Authors: domains cover only a slice of where RAG is deployed.
Authors: questions are strictly fact-based, with no multi-step logic, synthesis or higher-level reasoning.
Authors: dataset has an enriched rate of contextual errors, so metrics are not bias rates in the wild.
Authors: token-probability method only applies to models that expose probabilities (three of six).
Not shown: effect of model size, effect of fine-tuning, decoding settings, seeds or repeats, how responses are matched to answers.
Data is synthetic: questions, quality filtering and some perturbed excerpts come from GPT-4o, which is also evaluated.
Prompt-strength experiment is only a figure with a single model, no numbers.
Models are dated (GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Flash, Llama-3).
